question: At what height above a lower level does OSHA require fall protection for construction workers on an unprotected side or edge?
reference_answer: At 6 feet or more. The worker must be protected by guardrail systems, safety net systems or personal fall arrest systems.
agent_answer: OSHA requires fall protection for each employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet or more above a lower level [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501]. Employers must protect workers using guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501].

question: What roof slope counts as a steep roof?
reference_answer: A roof with a slope greater than 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal).
agent_answer: A steep roof is defined as a roof having a slope greater than 4 in 12 (vertical to horizontal) [1926-subpart-M | 1926.500].

question: How high must the top rail of a guardrail system be above the walking surface?
reference_answer: 42 inches, plus or minus 3 inches, above the walking/working level.
agent_answer: The top edge height of top rails for standard guardrail systems must be 42 inches plus or minus 3 inches above the walking or working level, though the height may exceed 45 inches when conditions warrant provided the system meets all other criteria [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502]. When employees are using stilts, the top rail height must be increased by an amount equal to the height of the stilts [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502]. For scaffolds, different height requirements apply depending on when the scaffold was placed in service and the type of scaffold [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: What is the most force a personal fall arrest system may put on a worker wearing a body harness when it stops a fall?
reference_answer: 1,800 pounds.
agent_answer: When stopping a fall, a personal fall arrest system must limit the maximum arresting force on an employee to 1,800 pounds (8 kN) when used with a body harness [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502].

question: How far below the working surface can a safety net be installed at the most?
reference_answer: As close as practicable under the working surface and never more than 30 feet below it.
agent_answer: Safety nets must be installed as close as practicable under the walking/working surface, but in no case more than 30 feet (9.1 m) below that level [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502].

question: How much weight must an anchorage for personal fall arrest equipment be able to support?
reference_answer: At least 5,000 pounds per employee attached, or it must be designed with a safety factor of at least two under a qualified person.
agent_answer: Anchorages used for the attachment of personal fall arrest equipment must be capable of supporting at least 5,000 pounds (22.2 kN) per employee attached, or else be designed, installed, and used under qualified supervision as part of a complete system that maintains a safety factor of at least two [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502]. Additionally, these anchorages must be independent of any anchorage being used to support or suspend platforms [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502].

question: What must the written certification of fall protection training contain?
reference_answer: The name or other identity of the employee trained, the date or dates of the training, and the signature of the trainer or the employer.
agent_answer: The written certification record of fall protection training must contain the name or other identity of the employee trained, the date or dates of the training, and the signature of the person who conducted the training or the signature of the employer [1926-subpart-M | 1926.503]. If the employer relies on training conducted by another employer or completed prior to the effective date of the section, the record must indicate the date the employer determined the prior training was adequate instead of the date of actual training [1926-subpart-M | 1926.503].

question: How deep must a trench be before a ladder, stairway or ramp for getting out is required, and how close to workers must it be?
reference_answer: At 4 feet or more in depth. It must be placed so workers need no more than 25 feet of lateral travel to reach it.
agent_answer: A stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress must be located in trench excavations that are 4 feet (1.22 m) or more in depth [1926-subpart-P | 1926.651]. It must be placed so that it requires no more than 25 feet (7.62 m) of lateral travel for employees [1926-subpart-P | 1926.651].

question: How far from the edge of an excavation must dug-out soil and equipment be kept?
reference_answer: At least 2 feet from the edge, or else retaining devices must be used.
agent_answer: Excavated materials and equipment must be placed and kept at least 2 feet (.61 m) from the edge of excavations, or retaining devices must be used that are sufficient to prevent them from falling or rolling in [1926-subpart-P | 1926.651].

question: When does an excavation not need a protective system against cave-ins?
reference_answer: When it is made entirely in stable rock, or when it is less than 5 feet deep and a competent person finds no indication of a possible cave-in.
agent_answer: An excavation does not need a protective system against cave-ins when the excavation is made entirely in stable rock [1926-subpart-P | 1926.652]. It is also exempt when the excavation is less than 5 feet in depth and an examination of the ground by a competent person provides no indication of a potential cave-in [1926-subpart-P | 1926.652].

question: What is the maximum allowable slope for Type C soil?
reference_answer: 1.5 horizontal to 1 vertical (34 degrees).
agent_answer: The maximum allowable slope for simple slope excavations 20 feet or less in depth in Type C soil is 1 1/2:1 (horizontal to vertical) [1926-subpart-P | Appendix B to Subpart P].

question: What unconfined compressive strength does Type A soil have?
reference_answer: 1.5 tons per square foot (144 kPa) or greater.
agent_answer: Type A soil has an unconfined compressive strength of 1.5 tons per square foot (tsf) (144 kPa) or greater [1926-subpart-P | Appendix A to Subpart P].

question: How much weight must a scaffold and its parts be able to support?
reference_answer: Its own weight and at least 4 times the maximum intended load applied to it.
agent_answer: Each scaffold and scaffold component must be capable of supporting, without failure, its own weight and at least 4 times the maximum intended load applied or transmitted to it [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: At what height above a lower level must workers on a scaffold be protected from falling?
reference_answer: More than 10 feet.
agent_answer: Each employee on a scaffold more than 10 feet (3.1 m) above a lower level must be protected from falling [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: How wide may the gap between scaffold platform units be?
reference_answer: No more than 1 inch, unless the employer can show a wider space is necessary.
agent_answer: The space between adjacent scaffold platform units must be no more than 1 inch (2.5 cm) wide, except when the employer demonstrates that a wider space is necessary, such as to fit around uprights when using side brackets [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451]. When a wider space is necessary, the open space between the platform and the uprights must not exceed 9 1/2 inches (24.1 cm) [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: When does a scaffold have to be inspected, and by whom?
reference_answer: By a competent person before each work shift and after any occurrence that could affect its structural integrity.
agent_answer: Scaffolds and scaffold components must be inspected for visible defects by a competent person before each work shift, and after any occurrence that could affect the structural integrity of the scaffold [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: How close may a scaffold get to an insulated power line carrying less than 300 volts?
reference_answer: No closer than 3 feet.
agent_answer: A scaffold may get no closer than 3 feet (0.9 m) to an insulated power line carrying less than 300 volts [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: How far must a portable ladder extend above the upper landing it is used to reach?
reference_answer: The side rails must extend at least 3 feet above the upper landing surface.
agent_answer:
When portable ladders are used for access to an upper landing surface, the ladder side rails must extend at least 3 feet above the upper landing surface [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053]. 

When such an extension is not possible because of the ladder's length, the ladder must be secured at its top to a rigid support that will not deflect, and a grasping device such as a grabrail must be provided to assist employees in mounting and dismounting [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053]. In no case shall the extension be such that ladder deflection under a load would, by itself, cause the ladder to slip off its support [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053].

question: When is a stairway or ladder required at a point of access on a construction site?
reference_answer: Where there is a break in elevation of 19 inches or more and no ramp, runway, sloped embankment or personnel hoist is provided.
agent_answer: A stairway or ladder must be provided at all personnel points of access where there is a break in elevation of 19 inches (48 cm) or more, provided that no ramp, runway, sloped embankment, or personnel hoist is provided [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1051].

question: At what angle should a non-self-supporting ladder be set up?
reference_answer: The horizontal distance from the top support to the foot of the ladder should be about one quarter of the ladder's working length.
agent_answer: Non-self-supporting ladders shall be used at an angle such that the horizontal distance from the top support to the foot of the ladder is approximately one-quarter of the working length of the ladder, which is the distance along the ladder between the foot and the top support [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053]. Additionally, wood job-made ladders with spliced side rails shall be used at an angle such that the horizontal distance is one-eighth the working length of the ladder [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053].

question: What head protection is required where there is a danger of head injury from falling objects?
reference_answer: Employees must be protected by protective helmets.
agent_answer: Employees working in areas where there is a possible danger of head injury from falling or flying objects must be protected by protective helmets [1926-subpart-E | 1926.100]. When an employee is exposed to falling objects, the employer shall have each employee wear a hard hat and implement specific measures such as toeboards, screens, guardrail systems, canopy structures, or barricades [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501].

question: When may concrete forms and shores be removed?
reference_answer: Once the employer determines the concrete has gained enough strength to support its weight and loads, based on following the plans and specifications or on ASTM compressive strength test results.
agent_answer:
Forms and shores, except those used for slabs on grade and slip forms, may be removed only after the employer determines that the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its weight and superimposed loads [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.703]. 

This determination must be based on compliance with one of the following conditions:
- The plans and specifications stipulate conditions for removal of forms and shores, and those conditions have been followed [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.703].
- The concrete has been properly tested with an appropriate ASTM standard test method designed to indicate concrete compressive strength, and the test results indicate that the concrete has gained sufficient strength to support its weight and superimposed loads [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.703].

question: How large must the limited access zone be when a masonry wall is being built?
reference_answer: The height of the wall plus 4 feet, running the entire length of the wall.
agent_answer: The limited access zone must be equal to the height of the wall to be constructed plus four feet, and must run the entire length of the wall [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.706]. It must be established on the side of the wall that will be unscaffolded before construction begins, and it must remain restricted to employees actively engaged in constructing the wall [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.706].

question: What must be done with protruding reinforcing steel that workers could fall onto?
reference_answer: It must be guarded to eliminate the hazard of impalement.
agent_answer: All protruding reinforcing steel, onto and into which employees could fall, must be guarded to eliminate the hazard of impalement [1926-subpart-Q | 1926.701].

question: How often must a competent person inspect an excavation?
reference_answer: Before work starts and as needed through the shift, and also after every rainstorm or other event that increases hazards.
agent_answer: A competent person must make daily inspections of excavations, adjacent areas, and protective systems prior to the start of work and as needed throughout the shift [1926-subpart-P | 1926.651]. Inspections must also be conducted after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing occurrence, and these inspections are only required when employee exposure can be reasonably anticipated [1926-subpart-P | 1926.651].

question: Which temporary power outlets on a construction site need ground-fault circuit interrupters?
reference_answer: All 120-volt, single-phase, 15 and 20 ampere receptacle outlets that are not part of the building's permanent wiring and are in use by employees.
agent_answer: All 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacle outlets on construction sites that are not part of the permanent wiring of the building or structure and are in use by employees must have approved ground-fault circuit interrupters for personnel protection, unless an assured equipment grounding conductor program is used instead [1926-subpart-K | 1926.404]. An exception is made for receptacles on a two-wire, single-phase portable or vehicle-mounted generator rated at not more than 5kW, where the circuit conductors of the generator are insulated from the generator frame and all other grounded surfaces [1926-subpart-K | 1926.404].

question: Can a worker be allowed to work close enough to an electric power circuit to touch it?
reference_answer: Not unless the worker is protected from shock by de-energizing and grounding the circuit or by guarding it effectively with insulation or other means.
agent_answer: No employer shall permit an employee to work in such proximity to any part of an electric power circuit that the employee could contact it in the course of work, unless the employee is protected against electric shock by deenergizing the circuit and grounding it or by guarding it effectively by insulation or other means [1926-subpart-K | 1926.416].

question: A crew is working on a low-slope roof 20 feet up. Which fall protection options are allowed, and how far from the roof edge must a warning line be when no mechanical equipment is in use?
reference_answer: Guardrail, safety net or personal fall arrest systems, or a warning line system combined with one of those or with a safety monitoring system. With no mechanical equipment the warning line must be at least 6 feet from the roof edge.
agent_answer: On a low-slope roof, employees engaged in roofing activities must be protected by guardrail systems, safety net systems, personal fall arrest systems, a combination of a warning line system and guardrail, safety net, personal fall arrest, or safety monitoring system, or on roofs 50 feet or less in width, a safety monitoring system alone [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501]. When no mechanical equipment is in use, the warning line must be erected not less than 6 feet from the roof edge [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502].

question: A 7-foot-deep trench is dug in soil with an unconfined compressive strength of 1 ton per square foot. What soil type is it, and how steep may the sides be if they are sloped?
reference_answer: Type B soil (strength above 0.5 and below 1.5 tons per square foot). The maximum allowable slope is 1 horizontal to 1 vertical (45 degrees).
agent_answer: A cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength greater than 0.5 tsf but less than 1.5 tsf is classified as Type B soil [1926-subpart-P | Appendix A to Subpart P]. For a simple slope excavation 20 feet or less in depth, the maximum allowable slope is 1:1 (horizontal to vertical) [1926-subpart-P | Appendix B to Subpart P].

question: Workers on a scaffold 15 feet above the ground need what fall protection, and what training must they have had?
reference_answer: They must be protected from falling (with guardrails or a personal fall arrest system depending on the scaffold type), and they must have been trained by a qualified person to recognize the scaffold hazards and how to deal with them.
agent_answer:
Each employee on a scaffold more than 10 feet above a lower level must be protected from falling by specified types of fall protection (such as personal fall arrest systems or guardrail systems, depending on the specific scaffold type) [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451]. 

Employers must have each employee who performs work on a scaffold trained by a qualified person to recognize the associated hazards (including electrical, fall, and falling object hazards) and understand the procedures to control or minimize them [1926-subpart-L | 1926.454]. If employees are involved in erecting, disassembling, moving, operating, repairing, maintaining, or inspecting a scaffold, they must be trained by a competent person on the correct procedures and design criteria for that scaffold type [1926-subpart-L | 1926.454].

question: A worker climbs a portable ladder to a roof edge 8 feet above the ground. How far must the ladder extend above the roof, and does the worker need fall protection at the edge?
reference_answer: The ladder side rails must extend at least 3 feet above the landing. Yes, an unprotected edge 6 feet or more above a lower level needs guardrails, a safety net or a personal fall arrest system.
agent_answer:
When portable ladders are used for access to an upper landing surface, the ladder side rails shall extend at least 3 feet (.9 m) above the upper landing surface to which the ladder is used to gain access [1926-subpart-X | 1926.1053]. 

Each employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501]. Because the roof edge is 8 feet above the ground, fall protection is required.

question: How does the required top rail height for scaffold guardrails compare with the height for ordinary guardrail systems?
reference_answer: Ordinary guardrail top rails are 42 inches plus or minus 3 inches (39 to 45). On supported scaffolds placed in service after January 1, 2000, the top edge must be between 38 and 45 inches.
agent_answer:
For ordinary guardrail systems, the top edge height of top rails must be 42 inches plus or minus 3 inches above the walking/working level [1926-subpart-M | 1926.502]. 

For scaffold guardrails, the required top rail height depends on when the scaffold was placed in service and the type of scaffold:
- Supported scaffolds manufactured or placed in service after January 1, 2000, must have toprails installed between 38 inches and 45 inches above the platform surface [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].
- Supported scaffolds manufactured and placed in service before January 1, 2000, and all suspended scaffolds requiring both a guardrail and a personal fall arrest system, must have toprails between 36 inches and 45 inches above the platform surface [1926-subpart-L | 1926.451].

question: An 8-foot-deep excavation next to a path is hidden by tall weeds. How must people be kept from falling in, and where must the dug-out soil go?
reference_answer: Guardrails, fences or barricades are required at the edge of an excavation 6 feet or more deep that is not readily seen. Soil and equipment must be kept at least 2 feet from the edge or be held back by retaining devices.
agent_answer:
Each employee at the edge of an excavation 6 feet or more in depth that is not readily seen because of plant growth or other visual barriers must be protected from falling by guardrail systems, fences, or barricades [1926-subpart-M | 1926.501]. 

Excavated or other materials must be placed and kept at least 2 feet from the edge of the excavation, or kept back by retaining devices sufficient to prevent materials from falling or rolling in, or by a combination of both [1926-subpart-P | 1926.651].

reference_answer: NOT IN CORPUS: steel erection (Subpart R) is not in the indexed subparts, so no connector height is given.

reference_answer: NOT IN CORPUS: the noise limits table is in Subpart D, which is not indexed. The hearing protection section only points to it.

question: After how many years must a safety harness be retired?
reference_answer: NOT IN CORPUS: the text requires inspection before each use and removal of defective parts, but sets no age limit.
agent_answer: NOT IN CORPUS: The retrieved standards in 29 CFR Part 1926 do not specify a fixed number of years after which a safety harness must be retired. The regulations instead require that any safety belt, lanyard, or personal fall arrest system component subjected to in-service loading must be immediately removed from service [1926-subpart-E | 1926.104], and components must be inspected regularly for defects, damage, or deterioration and withdrawn from service immediately if significant defects are found [1926-subpart-M | Appendix C to Subpart M]. Specific time-based expiration or retirement limits are typically established by equipment manufacturers rather than OSHA construction standards.

reference_answer: NOT IN CORPUS: general industry rules (29 CFR 1910) are not in the corpus, which covers construction only.

question: How many hours of fall protection training must a construction worker complete?
reference_answer: NOT IN CORPUS: the training section lists what the training must cover and the records to keep, but gives no number of hours.
agent_answer: NOT IN CORPUS: The regulations require employers to provide a training program for each employee exposed to fall hazards and specify what topics must be covered, but they do not state a specific number of required training hours [1926-subpart-M | 1926.503].
